tiles.label: Jupiter
tiles.quote: Jupiter was the chief god of the ancient Roman state religion, god of the sky and thunder, identified with the Greek Zeus

tiles.label: Mars
tiles.quote: Mars was the Roman god of war and, in early times, also a guardian of farmland, second in importance only to Jupiter in the state religion

tiles.label: Neptune
tiles.quote: Neptune was the Roman god of fresh water and the sea, identified with the Greek Poseidon

tiles.label: Minerva
tiles.quote: Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom, crafts and strategic war, identified with the Greek Athena

tiles.label: Diana
tiles.quote: Diana was the Roman goddess of hunting, wild animals, the moon and childbirth, later identified with the Greek Artemis

tiles.label: Saturn
tiles.quote: Saturn was an ancient Roman god of agriculture and wealth, identified with the Greek Kronos, whose festival, the Saturnalia, was held in December

tiles.label: Achilles
tiles.quote: Achilles is the greatest Greek warrior of the Trojan War in Greek legend and the central figure of Homer's Iliad

tiles.label: Odysseus
tiles.quote: Odysseus, called Ulysses by the Romans, is the legendary king of Ithaca in Greek myth, a hero of the Trojan War famous for his cunning, credited with the stratagem of the wooden horse

tiles.label: Agamemnon
tiles.quote: Agamemnon is the legendary king of Mycenae who, in Homer's Iliad, led the Greek army against Troy

tiles.label: Menelaus
tiles.quote: When Helen left with the Trojan prince Paris, he and Agamemnon led the Greek expedition against Troy

tiles.label: Helen
tiles.quote: Her abduction or flight with the Trojan prince Paris caused the Trojan War, told in the Homeric epics

tiles.label: Ajax
tiles.quote: Ajax the Great is a hero of Greek mythology, son of Telamon king of Salamis, who fights in the Trojan War in Homer's Iliad as the mightiest Greek warrior after Achilles

name: Queens of ancient Egypt

tiles.label: Hatshepsut
tiles.quote: Hatshepsut was a female pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt who ruled c

tiles.label: Nefertari
tiles.quote: Nefertari, also Nefertari Meritmut, was an Egyptian queen and the first of the Great Royal Wives of Ramesses the Great, whom she married before he became king

tiles.label: Tiye
tiles.quote: Tiye was the Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian pharaoh Amenhotep III, mother of Akhenaten and grandmother of Tutankhamun

tiles.label: Cleopatra
tiles.quote: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Empire, reigning from 51 to 30 BCE

tiles.label: Sobekneferu
tiles.quote: Sobekneferu was the last ruler of the Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt, reigning for nearly four years in the late nineteenth century BCE

tiles.label: Tausret
tiles.quote: Tausret, also spelled Tawosret or Twosret, was the last known ruler of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt

note: Cleopatra is also in Julius Caesar's world

tiles.label: Mark Antony
tiles.quote: Mark Antony was a Roman general and politician, an ally of Julius Caesar and later a member of the Second Triumvirate

tiles.label: Vercingetorix
tiles.quote: Vercingetorix was a chief of the Arverni who in 52 BCE united most of the Gauls in revolt against Julius Caesar

tiles.label: Brutus
tiles.quote: Marcus Junius Brutus was a Roman senator who, with Gaius Cassius Longinus, led the conspiracy that killed Julius Caesar on the Ides of March 44 BCE

tiles.label: Caesarion
tiles.quote: Caesarion, formally Ptolemy XV, was the son of Cleopatra VII and, by her account, of Julius Caesar

tiles.label: Rubicon
tiles.quote: The crossing of the Rubicon was Julius Caesar's decision in 49 BCE to lead his army across the Rubicon River in northern Italy, the boundary of his province, in defiance of the Senate

tiles.label: Julian calendar
tiles.quote: The Julian calendar is a solar calendar introduced by Julius Caesar in 46 BCE, with a leap year every four years

name: The eruption of Vesuvius

tiles.label: Pompeii
tiles.quote: Pompeii was an ancient town in Campania, southern Italy, near the Bay of Naples, buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE

tiles.label: Herculaneum
tiles.quote: Herculaneum was an ancient Roman town on the Bay of Naples, at modern Ercolano, buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE

tiles.label: Stabiae
tiles.quote: Destroyed by Sulla in 89 BCE during the Social War, it became a resort of large seaside villas, which were buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE

tiles.label: Pliny the Elder
tiles.quote: He died while commanding the fleet at Misenum during the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE.

tiles.label: Pliny the Younger
tiles.quote: His published letters describe Roman public and private life, including the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE

tiles.label: Titus
tiles.quote: As emperor he dealt with the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 and opened the Colosseum in 80.

note: Titus is a decoy for Roman emperors

tiles.label: Genesis
tiles.quote: The Book of Genesis is the first book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, recounting the creation of the world, the Flood and the stories of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph

tiles.label: Exodus
tiles.quote: The Book of Exodus is the second book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the Israelites' departure from Egypt and the giving of the law at Sinai

tiles.label: Psalms
tiles.quote: The Book of Psalms is a collection of 150 religious poems and songs in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, composed over several centuries and traditionally attributed in large part to King David

tiles.label: Ecclesiastes
tiles.quote: Ecclesiastes is a book of the Hebrew Bible, part of its wisdom literature, presented as the reflections of Qoheleth, the Preacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, traditionally identified with Solomon

tiles.label: Song of Songs
tiles.quote: The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon, is a book of the Hebrew Bible consisting of love poems in the voices of a woman and her lover

tiles.label: Proverbs
tiles.quote: The Book of Proverbs is a book of the Hebrew Bible, part of its wisdom literature, made up of collections of moral and practical sayings

tiles.label: Moses
tiles.quote: According to the Hebrew Bible he led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt and received the law, including the Ten Commandments, from God at Mount Sinai, and the first five books of the Bible are traditionally attributed to him

tiles.label: Samson
tiles.quote: Samson is a hero of the Book of Judges in the Hebrew Bible, a Nazirite of the tribe of Dan endowed with great strength

tiles.label: Goliath
tiles.quote: Goliath is the Philistine giant of Gath in the Hebrew Bible, killed by the young David with a sling in the Valley of Elah in the story told in 1 Samuel 17

tiles.label: Bathsheba
tiles.quote: Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah the Hittite who, according to the Hebrew Bible, became the wife of King David after he committed adultery with her and arranged Uriah's death in battle

tiles.label: Jezebel
tiles.quote: Jezebel was a Phoenician princess, the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, who married King Ahab of Israel in the ninth century BCE

tiles.label: Ark of the Covenant
tiles.quote: The Ark of the Covenant is, in the Hebrew Bible, a gilded wooden chest holding the tablets of the Law given to Moses

tiles.label: Ishtar Gate
tiles.quote: The Ishtar Gate was a monumental gateway to the inner city of Babylon, built under Nebuchadnezzar II and dedicated to the goddess Ishtar

tiles.label: Hanging Gardens
tiles.quote: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were a legendary terraced garden listed among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

tiles.label: Etemenanki
tiles.quote: Etemenanki, 'temple of the foundation of heaven and earth', was the ziggurat of Marduk in Babylon, standing beside his temple Esagila

tiles.label: Esagila
tiles.quote: The Esagila was the great temple of Marduk in Babylon, the most important sanctuary of the city

tiles.label: Processional Way
tiles.quote: The Processional Way was a monumental street in Babylon leading through the Ishtar Gate, decorated with glazed brick reliefs of lions

tiles.label: Marduk
tiles.quote: Marduk was the chief god of Babylon, elevated to head of the Mesopotamian pantheon as Babylon's power grew

tiles.label: Giza
tiles.quote: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE

tiles.label: Djoser
tiles.quote: The Pyramid of Djoser, or Step Pyramid, is a six-stepped stone pyramid at Saqqara in Egypt, built for the Third Dynasty king Djoser in the 27th century BCE

tiles.label: Meidum
tiles.quote: Its pyramid, completed under Sneferu in the 26th century BCE, was converted from a step pyramid into a true pyramid and later lost much of its outer casing

tiles.label: Sun (Teotihuacan)
tiles.quote: The Pyramid of the Sun is the largest building at Teotihuacan and one of the largest pyramids of Mesoamerica, about 65 metres high, raised on the east side of the Avenue of the Dead and probably completed by about 200 CE

tiles.label: Moon (Teotihuacan)
tiles.quote: The Pyramid of the Moon is the second-largest pyramid of Teotihuacan, standing at the northern end of the Avenue of the Dead with Cerro Gordo behind it

tiles.label: Cholula
tiles.quote: The Great Pyramid of Cholula, Tlachihualtepetl, is a huge temple platform in the Puebla valley of Mexico, the largest pyramid in the world by volume

name: Empires of antiquity

tiles.label: Roman
tiles.quote: The Roman Empire was the state ruled by emperors from Rome after the end of the Roman Republic, at its height controlling the entire Mediterranean world and much of western Europe and the Near East

tiles.label: Achaemenid
tiles.quote: The Achaemenid Empire was the first Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in the sixth century BCE and stretching at its height from the Aegean to the Indus

tiles.label: Maurya
tiles.quote: The Maurya Empire was the first state to unite most of the Indian subcontinent, founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE

tiles.label: Han
tiles.quote: The Han Dynasty ruled China from 202 BCE to 220 CE, with a brief interruption, and is regarded as a formative era of Chinese civilisation

tiles.label: Kushan
tiles.quote: The Kushan Empire was a state founded by the Yuezhi in Bactria that expanded into northern India in the first centuries CE

tiles.label: Parthian
tiles.quote: The Parthian Empire, ruled by the Arsacid dynasty, was an Iranian state that emerged around 247 BCE and came to rule Iran and Mesopotamia

note: Broad: keep out of puzzles that hold another empire tile (Median, Chaldean, Gallic, Assyrian Empire in the year groups)

name: In the life of Alexander the Great

tiles.label: Philip II
tiles.quote: Philip II was king of Macedon from 359 to 336 BCE and the father of Alexander the Great

tiles.label: Olympias
tiles.quote: Olympias was a Molossian princess of Epirus, daughter of King Neoptolemus I, who married Philip II of Macedon and was the mother of Alexander the Great

tiles.label: Roxana
tiles.quote: Roxana was a Bactrian noblewoman, daughter of Oxyartes, whom Alexander the Great married in 327 BCE

tiles.label: Darius III
tiles.quote: He was defeated by Alexander the Great at the battles of Issus and Gaugamela and was killed by his own officers in 330 BCE while fleeing eastward

tiles.label: Alexandria
tiles.quote: Alexandria is a city on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BCE

tiles.label: Diadochi
tiles.quote: The Diadochi ('successors') were the generals and companions of Alexander the Great who fought over his empire after his death in 323 BCE

tiles.label: Forum
tiles.quote: The Roman Forum was the central public square of ancient Rome, in the valley between the Palatine and Capitoline hills

tiles.label: Capitoline
tiles.quote: The Capitoline Hill is one of the seven hills of Rome, overlooking the Forum

tiles.label: Trajan's Column
tiles.quote: Trajan's Column is a Roman triumphal column in Trajan's Forum in Rome, dedicated in 113 CE

tiles.label: Castel Sant'Angelo
tiles.quote: Castel Sant'Angelo is a fortress in Rome on the right bank of the Tiber, built in the second century as the mausoleum of the emperor Hadrian

tiles.label: Cloaca Maxima
tiles.quote: The Cloaca Maxima ('Greatest Sewer') is one of the oldest sewer systems in the world, built in ancient Rome to drain the marshy valley of the Forum into the Tiber

tiles.label: Aventine
tiles.quote: The Aventine is the southernmost of the seven hills of Rome, beside the Tiber

tiles.label: John the Baptist
tiles.quote: John the Baptist was a Jewish preacher active in the Jordan valley in the early 1st century CE, who called for repentance and baptised followers in the river, among them Jesus

tiles.label: Andrew
tiles.quote: Andrew the Apostle was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, the brother of Simon Peter and a fisherman from Galilee

tiles.label: Thomas
tiles.quote: Thomas the Apostle was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, remembered in the Gospel of John for doubting the resurrection until he saw Jesus

tiles.label: Herod Antipas
tiles.quote: He built Tiberias as his capital, had John the Baptist executed and appears in the Gospel accounts of Jesus's trial

tiles.label: Passion
tiles.quote: It is told in all four Gospels and is central to Christian worship, art and devotion, including the veneration of relics believed to come from it.

tiles.label: Gospel of John
tiles.quote: The Gospel of John is the fourth of the canonical gospels of the New Testament, probably written around 90–110 CE

tiles.label: Persepolis
tiles.quote: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, located in Fars in south-western Iran and begun under Darius I

tiles.label: Royal Road
tiles.quote: The Royal Road was an ancient highway of the Achaemenid Empire running about 2,700 kilometres from Susa to Sardis, with relay stations along its length

tiles.label: Satrapy
tiles.quote: A satrapy was a province of the Achaemenid Empire governed by a satrap, a royal governor responsible for taxation, security and administration

tiles.label: Immortals
tiles.quote: The Immortals were an elite force of the Achaemenid Persian army, described by Herodotus as numbering ten thousand

tiles.label: Daric
tiles.quote: The daric was a gold coin of the Achaemenid Empire, introduced under Darius I

tiles.label: Cyrus Cylinder
tiles.quote: The Cyrus Cylinder is an inscribed clay cylinder issued after the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE

name: Ancient inventions

tiles.label: Wheel
tiles.quote: before 4000 BCE

tiles.label: Coins
tiles.quote: 7th century BCE

tiles.label: Chariot
tiles.quote: A chariot is a light, two-wheeled, horse-drawn vehicle used in warfare, carrying a driver and an archer or spearman

tiles.label: Trireme
tiles.quote: c. 700 BCE

tiles.label: Aqueduct
tiles.quote: An aqueduct is a channel or structure built to carry water from a source to a city, often across valleys on arches

tiles.label: Sail
tiles.quote: 6th millennium BCE

note: Broad: keep apart from First known in Mesopotamia

tiles.label: Hadrian's Wall
tiles.quote: Hadrian's Wall is a Roman frontier wall across northern England from the Tyne to the Solway Firth, begun in 122 CE on the orders of Emperor Hadrian

tiles.label: Antonine Wall
tiles.quote: The Antonine Wall was a Roman turf rampart built across the Forth–Clyde isthmus of central Scotland from 142 on the orders of Emperor Antoninus Pius

tiles.label: Watling Street
tiles.quote: Watling Street is an ancient route in England and Wales, paved by the Romans as a main road from the Kent ports through London to Wroxeter

tiles.label: Fishbourne
tiles.quote: Fishbourne Roman Palace, near Chichester in West Sussex, is the largest known Roman residence in Britain, built around 75 with formal gardens and fine mosaics

tiles.label: Vindolanda
tiles.quote: Vindolanda was a Roman auxiliary fort in northern England, just south of Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland

tiles.label: Fosse Way
tiles.quote: The Fosse Way was a Roman road in Britain running about 370 kilometres from Exeter through Bath, Cirencester and Leicester to Lincoln

name: Carthaginians

tiles.label: Hannibal
tiles.quote: Hannibal Barca was a Carthaginian general who led the invasion of Italy during the Second Punic War

tiles.label: Hamilcar Barca
tiles.quote: Hamilcar Barca was a Carthaginian general who commanded in Sicily in the last years of the First Punic War and then crushed the Mercenary War in Africa

tiles.label: Hasdrubal Barca
tiles.quote: Hasdrubal Barca was a Carthaginian general, son of Hamilcar Barca and brother of Hannibal

tiles.label: Dido
tiles.quote: Dido, also called Elissa, was the legendary queen from Tyre who is said to have founded Carthage

tiles.label: Hanno
tiles.quote: Hanno the Navigator was a Carthaginian explorer who led a voyage along the Atlantic coast of West Africa around 500 BCE

tiles.label: Hasdrubal the Fair
tiles.quote: Hasdrubal the Fair was a Carthaginian general, son-in-law of Hamilcar Barca, who succeeded him as commander in Iberia in about 229 BCE

note: Hanno is also in Travellers of the ancient world; Dido is legendary

name: Athenians

tiles.label: Socrates
tiles.quote: Socrates was an Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing himself but questioned his fellow citizens about justice, virtue and knowledge, a method of inquiry known through the dialogues of his pupil Plato and the writings of Xenophon

tiles.label: Plato
tiles.quote: Plato was an Athenian philosopher of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, author of dialogues such as the Republic

tiles.label: Sophocles
tiles.quote: Sophocles was an Athenian tragic playwright who lived from about 497 to 406 BCE

tiles.label: Pericles
tiles.quote: Pericles was an Athenian statesman and general who dominated the democracy from the 450s until his death in 429 BCE

tiles.label: Aristophanes
tiles.quote: Aristophanes was an Athenian comic playwright, the chief representative of Old Comedy, whose eleven surviving plays include The Clouds, The Birds, Lysistrata and The Frogs

tiles.label: Thucydides
tiles.quote: Thucydides was an Athenian general and historian, author of the History of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta

note: Decoy: Aristotle was from Stagira, not Athens

tiles.label: Boudica
tiles.quote: Boudica was queen of the Iceni of eastern Britain who led a great revolt against Roman rule in 60 or 61 CE after the Romans seized her late husband's kingdom and mistreated her family

tiles.label: Zenobia
tiles.quote: She conquered Egypt in 270 and much of Anatolia, creating a breakaway Palmyrene Empire in Rome's East

tiles.label: Teuta
tiles.quote: Illyrian raids on Greek cities and Italian traders under her rule, and the killing of a Roman envoy, provoked the First Illyrian War in 229 BCE

tiles.label: Amanirenas
tiles.quote: Around 25 BCE her armies attacked Roman Egypt, sacking Syene and carrying off statues of Augustus, one of whose bronze heads was buried at Meroë

tiles.label: Artemisia I
tiles.quote: Herodotus, himself from Halicarnassus, describes how she commanded five ships in Xerxes' invasion of Greece and fought at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE, having advised the king against giving battle

tiles.label: Tomyris
tiles.quote: According to Herodotus, after Cyrus the Great of Persia captured her son by a trick, she defeated the Persian army in 530 BCE, killed Cyrus and had his head put in a wineskin filled with blood.

tiles.label: Romulus
tiles.quote: Romulus is the legendary founder and first king of Rome, said to have been suckled with his twin brother Remus by a she-wolf

tiles.label: Numa Pompilius
tiles.quote: Numa Pompilius was, according to Roman tradition, the second king of Rome, a Sabine from Cures chosen after Romulus

tiles.label: Tullus Hostilius
tiles.quote: Tullus Hostilius was the third of the legendary kings of Rome, traditionally reigning from 673 to 642 BCE

tiles.label: Tarquinius Priscus
tiles.quote: Lucius Tarquinius Priscus was, according to Roman tradition, the fifth king of Rome, reigning from 616 to 579 BCE

tiles.label: Servius Tullius
tiles.quote: Servius Tullius was, according to Roman tradition, the sixth king of Rome, reigning in the 6th century BCE

tiles.label: Tarquin the Proud
tiles.quote: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, Tarquin the Proud, was by tradition the seventh and last king of Rome

tiles.label: Panathenaea
tiles.quote: The Panathenaea was the chief festival of Athens, held each summer in honour of Athena Polias, with a grander version, the Great Panathenaia, every four years from 566 BCE

tiles.label: Dionysia
tiles.quote: The Dionysia were Athenian festivals of the god Dionysus, the greatest being the City Dionysia held each spring

tiles.label: Akitu
tiles.quote: Akitu was the Mesopotamian New Year festival, celebrated most famously at Babylon in honour of the god Marduk

tiles.label: Passover
tiles.quote: Passover is a major Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus of the Israelites from Egypt, celebrated in spring from the 15th day of the month of Nisan

tiles.label: Hanukkah
tiles.quote: Hanukkah is an eight-day Jewish festival beginning on 25 Kislev, usually in December

tiles.label: Thesmophoria
tiles.quote: The Thesmophoria was an ancient Greek religious festival in honour of the goddess Demeter and her daughter Persephone, held each year, mostly around the sowing of seed in late autumn, to promote human and agricultural fertility

tiles.label: Parthenon
tiles.quote: The Parthenon is the temple of Athena Parthenos on the Acropolis of Athens, built between 447 and 432 BCE under Pericles by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates, with sculpture supervised by Phidias

tiles.label: Erechtheion
tiles.quote: The Erechtheion is an Ionic temple on the Acropolis of Athens, built around 421–406 BCE and dedicated to Athena Polias, Poseidon and the legendary king Erechtheus

tiles.label: Propylaea
tiles.quote: The Propylaea is the monumental gateway to the Acropolis of Athens, built between 437 and 432 BCE to designs by the architect Mnesicles as part of the building programme of Pericles

tiles.label: Phidias
tiles.quote: Phidias was an Athenian sculptor, regarded in antiquity as the greatest of the Greeks, who supervised the sculpture of the Parthenon under Pericles

tiles.label: Areopagus
tiles.quote: The Areopagus was the ancient council of Athens, named after the hill north-west of the Acropolis where it met

tiles.label: Callicrates
tiles.quote: He is also credited with the small Ionic Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis and worked on the walls linking Athens to Piraeus.

tiles.label: Schliemann
tiles.quote: Heinrich Schliemann was a German businessman and pioneering archaeologist who set out to prove the historical basis of Homer's epics

tiles.label: Arthur Evans
tiles.quote: Sir Arthur Evans was a British archaeologist who excavated the Bronze Age palace at Knossos on Crete from 1900 and partly reconstructed it in concrete

tiles.label: Leonard Woolley
tiles.quote: Sir Leonard Woolley was a British archaeologist best known for excavating Ur in southern Iraq from 1922 to 1934

tiles.label: Layard
tiles.quote: Austen Henry Layard was a British archaeologist and diplomat who excavated the Assyrian capitals of Nimrud and Nineveh between 1845 and 1851, sending colossal winged bulls and palace reliefs to the British Museum

tiles.label: Hormuzd Rassam
tiles.quote: Hormuzd Rassam was an Assyriologist and diplomat, born in Mosul to an Assyrian Christian family, who worked as Austen Henry Layard's assistant and later excavated for the British Museum

tiles.label: Mortimer Wheeler
tiles.quote: Sir Mortimer Wheeler was a British archaeologist and army officer who directed the National Museum of Wales and the London Museum and in 1934 established the Institute of Archaeology in London

tiles.label: Appian Way
tiles.quote: The Appian Way (Via Appia) was a Roman road begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, first from Rome to Capua and later extended to Brundisium on the Adriatic

tiles.label: Via Egnatia
tiles.quote: The Via Egnatia was a Roman road built in the later 2nd century BCE by the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius after Macedonia became a province

tiles.label: Via Aemilia
tiles.quote: The Via Aemilia was a Roman road built in 187 BCE by the consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, running in a straight line along the northern edge of the Apennines from Ariminum (Rimini) to Placentia (Piacenza) on the Po

tiles.label: Via Augusta
tiles.quote: The Via Augusta was the longest Roman road in Hispania, running about 1,500 kilometres from the Pyrenees along the Mediterranean coast through Tarraco and Valentia and then inland to Corduba and Gades

tiles.label: Via Cassia
tiles.quote: The Via Cassia was a Roman road running north from Rome through Etruria, past Sutri, Viterbo and Arezzo to Florence and beyond

tiles.label: Ermine Street
tiles.quote: Ermine Street was a major Roman road in Britain running north from London through Lincoln to York, built in the early years after the conquest of 43 CE

tiles.label: Augustus
tiles.quote: Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and known as Octavian before 27 BCE, was the first Roman emperor

tiles.label: Tiberius
tiles.quote: Tiberius was the second Roman emperor, ruling from 14 to 37 CE as the stepson and adopted heir of Augustus

tiles.label: Caligula
tiles.quote: Caligula, properly Gaius Caesar, was Roman emperor from 37 to 41 CE, the son of Germanicus and successor of Tiberius

tiles.label: Claudius
tiles.quote: Claudius was Roman emperor from 41 to 54 CE, proclaimed by the Praetorian Guard after the murder of his nephew Caligula

tiles.label: Nero
tiles.quote: Nero was Roman emperor from 54 to 68 CE, the last of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, adopted heir of Claudius

tiles.label: Germanicus
tiles.quote: Germanicus Julius Caesar (15 BCE–19 CE) was a Roman general, nephew and adopted son of the emperor Tiberius

tiles.label: Philippi
tiles.quote: The forces of the Second Triumvirate under Mark Antony and Octavian defeated the army of Brutus and Cassius, assassins of Julius Caesar, in two engagements, after which both killed themselves

tiles.label: Actium
tiles.quote: The Battle of Actium was a naval battle fought in 31 BCE off western Greece between Octavian and the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII

tiles.label: Thapsus
tiles.quote: The Battle of Thapsus was fought on 6 April 46 BCE near Thapsus, on the coast of present-day Tunisia, between Julius Caesar and the Pompeian forces of Metellus Scipio, supported by King Juba I of Numidia

tiles.label: Colline Gate
tiles.quote: Sulla's army defeated a force of Samnites and Lucanians led by Pontius Telesinus, fighting with Roman opponents of Sulla, in a hard battle that lasted into the night, after which Sulla had thousands of prisoners killed

tiles.label: Munda
tiles.quote: The Battle of Munda was fought on 17 March 45 BCE in southern Spain between Julius Caesar and the Pompeian army of Gnaeus and Sextus Pompeius and Titus Labienus

tiles.label: Frigidus
tiles.quote: The eastern emperor Theodosius I defeated the western usurper Eugenius and his Frankish general Arbogast, helped by a strong wind, the bora, blowing in his soldiers' favour

name: Roman defeats

tiles.label: Cannae
tiles.quote: Hannibal's Carthaginian army encircled and destroyed a much larger Roman army

tiles.label: Teutoburg Forest
tiles.quote: The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest was fought in 9 CE in Germania, where Germanic tribes led by Arminius ambushed and destroyed three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus

tiles.label: Carrhae
tiles.quote: A Parthian army of horse archers and heavy cavalry under the general Surena destroyed a Roman army led by Marcus Licinius Crassus, who was killed

tiles.label: Adrianople
tiles.quote: The Battle of Adrianople was fought in 378 CE in Thrace between the Roman army under the eastern emperor Valens and Gothic forces

tiles.label: Caudine Forks
tiles.quote: The Battle of the Caudine Forks in 321 BCE was a Roman disaster of the Second Samnite War

tiles.label: Edessa
tiles.quote: The Battle of Edessa was fought in 260 CE in upper Mesopotamia between the Roman emperor Valerian and the Sasanian king Shapur I

note: Adrianople is also in Battles of the Migration Period

tiles.label: Theodora
tiles.quote: Theodora was a Byzantine empress, wife of Emperor Justinian I and one of the most influential women in Byzantine history

tiles.label: Belisarius
tiles.quote: Belisarius was the leading general of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I

tiles.label: Procopius
tiles.quote: His 'History of the Wars' describes Justinian's campaigns against Persia, the Vandals and the Ostrogoths and is the main source for many peoples on the empire's frontiers

tiles.label: Hagia Sophia
tiles.quote: The Hagia Sophia is a great domed church in Constantinople completed in 537 CE under the emperor Justinian I

tiles.label: Corpus Juris Civilis
tiles.quote: The Corpus Juris Civilis is the body of Roman law compiled on the orders of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, completed in 534 CE

tiles.label: Narses
tiles.quote: Narses was an Armenian eunuch who rose to high office at the court of Justinian I and became one of his leading generals

tiles.label: Alcibiades
tiles.quote: He promoted the Sicilian Expedition of 415 BCE, deserted to Sparta when accused of sacrilege, and later returned to lead the Athenian fleet to victories such as Cyzicus in 410 BCE

tiles.label: Lysander
tiles.quote: Lysander was a Spartan admiral and statesman who won the Peloponnesian War for Sparta

tiles.label: Brasidas
tiles.quote: Brasidas was a Spartan general of the Peloponnesian War

tiles.label: Nicias
tiles.quote: He was largely responsible for the Peace of Nicias with Sparta in 421

tiles.label: Sphacteria
tiles.quote: The Battle of Sphacteria was fought in 425 BCE on the island of Sphacteria, which closes the bay of Pylos in Messenia, during the Peloponnesian War

tiles.label: Sicilian Expedition
tiles.quote: The Sicilian Expedition was the Athenian invasion of Sicily during the Peloponnesian War, launched in 415 BCE on the pretext of aiding Segesta against Selinus and aimed at Syracuse

tiles.label: Charioteer of Delphi
tiles.quote: The Charioteer of Delphi is a life-size bronze statue of a chariot driver made around 475 BCE, part of a group dedicated at Delphi by Polyzalus, tyrant of Gela in Sicily, for a victory in the Pythian Games

tiles.label: Venus de Milo
tiles.quote: The Venus de Milo, or Aphrodite of Milos, is an ancient Greek marble statue of a goddess, usually identified as Aphrodite, found on the island of Melos in 1820

tiles.label: Dying Gaul
tiles.quote: The Dying Gaul is an ancient marble statue of a wounded Celtic warrior, now in the Capitoline Museums in Rome

tiles.label: Motya Charioteer
tiles.quote: The Motya Charioteer is a marble statue of a young man in a long, finely pleated tunic, found in 1979 on the island of Motya off western Sicily

tiles.label: Hermes of Andros
tiles.quote: The Hermes of Andros is a marble statue of the god Hermes as guide of souls, found in 1832 at Palaiopolis, the ancient city of Andros, in the Cyclades

tiles.label: Colossus of Rhodes
tiles.quote: The Colossus of Rhodes was a bronze statue of the sun god Helios, about 33 metres high, made by Chares of Lindos to celebrate the city's survival of the siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305–304 BCE

name: Sacked Rome

tiles.label: Visigoths
tiles.quote: They destroyed a Roman army and killed Emperor Valens at Adrianople in 378 CE, and under Alaric they sacked Rome in 410 CE

tiles.label: Vandals
tiles.quote: They established a kingdom centred on Carthage and sacked Rome in 455 CE

tiles.label: Celts
tiles.quote: Associated with the Hallstatt and La Tène cultures, they sacked Rome around 390 BCE, invaded Greece in 279 BCE and settled in Galatia

tiles.label: Alaric
tiles.quote: In 410 his forces sacked Rome, the first time the city had fallen to a foreign enemy in about eight centuries

tiles.label: Brennus
tiles.quote: Brennus was a chieftain of the Senones, a Gallic people of northern Italy, who according to Roman tradition defeated the Roman army at the Allia and sacked Rome in 390 BCE (about 387 BCE by modern reckoning)

tiles.label: Duke of Bourbon
tiles.quote: He commanded imperial troops at Pavia and was killed leading the attack on Rome in 1527, which became the Sack of Rome.

note: The Duke of Bourbon (1527) is the odd one out in time; his entry says he was killed leading the attack that became the Sack of Rome

tiles.label: Olympia
tiles.quote: Olympia was a sanctuary of Zeus in the western Peloponnese, in the valley of the Alpheios in Elis, where the Olympic Games were held, traditionally from 776 BCE

tiles.label: Dodona
tiles.quote: Dodona in Epirus, north-western Greece, was the oldest oracle of the Greek world, sacred to Zeus and Dione

tiles.label: Eleusis
tiles.quote: It was home to the sanctuary of Demeter and Persephone where the Eleusinian Mysteries, the most famous secret religious rites of the Greek world, were celebrated for many centuries

tiles.label: Didyma
tiles.quote: Didyma was a sanctuary of Apollo on the west coast of Asia Minor, about 16 kilometres south of Miletus, which controlled it and was linked to it by a Sacred Way

tiles.label: Claros
tiles.quote: Claros was an ancient sanctuary and oracle of Apollo in Ionia, on the west coast of Asia Minor, in the territory of Colophon near modern Ahmetbeyli in Turkey

tiles.label: Argive Heraion
tiles.quote: The Argive Heraion was the chief sanctuary of the goddess Hera in the Argolid in southern Greece, on a hillside between Argos and Mycenae

name: Travellers of the ancient world

tiles.label: Pytheas
tiles.quote: Pytheas was a Greek navigator and geographer from Massalia, modern Marseille, who made a voyage to north-western Europe around 325 BCE

tiles.label: Zhang Qian
tiles.quote: Zhang Qian was a Han dynasty envoy sent west by Emperor Wu around 138 BCE to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu

tiles.label: Faxian
tiles.quote: Faxian was a Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled to India in search of Buddhist texts, a journey that lasted from 399 to 412, about ten years of it in India

tiles.label: Megasthenes
tiles.quote: Megasthenes was a Greek historian and diplomat sent by the Seleucid king Seleucus I as envoy to the court of Chandragupta Maurya at Pataliputra around 300 BCE

tiles.label: Hanno
tiles.quote: Hanno the Navigator was a Carthaginian explorer who led a voyage along the Atlantic coast of West Africa around 500 BCE

tiles.label: Xuanzang
tiles.quote: Xuanzang was a Chinese Buddhist monk, scholar and traveller who journeyed overland to India between 629 and 645 to collect scriptures

note: Xuanzang travelled 629-645, just past the period

tiles.label: Melqart
tiles.quote: Melqart was the chief god of the Phoenician city of Tyre, whose name means 'king of the city'

tiles.label: Eshmun
tiles.quote: Eshmun was the Phoenician god of healing and the chief god of Sidon

tiles.label: Tanit
tiles.quote: Tanit was the chief goddess of Carthage and the Punic world, often paired with the god Baal Hammon and called 'face of Baal'

tiles.label: Baal Hammon
tiles.quote: Baal Hammon was the chief god of Carthage and the Punic world, worshipped with the goddess Tanit

tiles.label: Astarte
tiles.quote: Astarte was a major goddess of the ancient Levant, worshipped by Phoenicians, Canaanites and others as a deity of love, fertility and war

tiles.label: Baal
tiles.quote: Baal, meaning lord, was the title of the Canaanite storm and fertility god Hadad, widely worshipped in the ancient Levant

tiles.label: Edict of Milan
tiles.quote: The Edict of Milan was the agreement of 313 CE between the emperors Constantine and Licinius granting religious toleration throughout the Roman Empire, including to Christians

tiles.label: Council of Nicaea
tiles.quote: The First Council of Nicaea was a gathering of Christian bishops called by the emperor Constantine I at Nicaea in Bithynia in 325

tiles.label: Licinius
tiles.quote: In 313 he and Constantine the Great agreed the policy of religious toleration known as the Edict of Milan, and he went on to defeat Maximinus Daia and rule the eastern provinces

tiles.label: Constantinople
tiles.quote: Constantinople, now Istanbul, was the city on the Bosphorus refounded by Constantine I in the fourth century CE on the site of Byzantion

tiles.label: Arius
tiles.quote: The Council of Nicaea condemned his views in 325, but Arianism remained influential for decades and was adopted by the Goths and other Germanic peoples

tiles.label: Constantius I
tiles.quote: He died at York in 306, where his troops proclaimed his son Constantine emperor.

tiles.label: Jugurthine
tiles.quote: The Jugurthine War was fought from 112 to 105 BCE between the Roman Republic and Jugurtha, king of Numidia

tiles.label: Cimbrian
tiles.quote: The Cimbrian War was fought from 113 to 101 BCE between the Roman Republic and the migrating Cimbri and Teutones

tiles.label: Sertorian
tiles.quote: The Sertorian War was a Roman civil war fought in Hispania from 80 to 72 BCE between Quintus Sertorius, a supporter of the Marian party, and the government in Rome established by Sulla

tiles.label: Social War
tiles.quote: The Social War was the revolt of Rome's Italian allies, led by the Marsi and Samnites, who demanded Roman citizenship

tiles.label: Latin War
tiles.quote: The Latin War of 340–338 BCE was fought between Rome and its former allies of the Latin League, joined by the Campanians and Volsci

tiles.label: Samnite Wars
tiles.quote: The Samnite Wars were three wars fought between the Roman Republic and the Samnites of the southern Apennines between 343 and 290 BCE

name: Battles of the Migration Period

tiles.label: Adrianople
tiles.quote: The disaster allowed the Goths to settle within the empire and is often regarded as a turning point in the decline of the Roman Empire.

tiles.label: Catalaunian Plains
tiles.quote: The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains was fought in 451 in north-eastern Gaul between the Hunnic army of Attila and a coalition led by the Roman general Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I

tiles.label: Nedao
tiles.quote: The Battle of Nedao was fought in 454 in Pannonia between the sons of Attila and a coalition of their former subject peoples led by the Gepid king Ardaric

tiles.label: Vouillé
tiles.quote: Clovis I and his Franks defeated the Visigoths, whose king Alaric II was killed, according to Gregory of Tours by Clovis himself

tiles.label: Tolbiac
tiles.quote: The Battle of Tolbiac was fought around 496 at or near Tolbiacum (Zülpich), west of Cologne, between the Franks under Clovis I and the Alemanni

tiles.label: Vézeronce
tiles.quote: The Battle of Vézeronce was fought on 25 June 524 near Vézeronce in the Dauphiné, France, between the Franks and the Burgundians

note: Adrianople is also a Roman defeat

name: Gods of healing

tiles.label: Asclepius
tiles.quote: Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine, a son of Apollo, whose symbol was a staff with a serpent coiled around it

tiles.label: Eshmun
tiles.quote: Eshmun was the Phoenician god of healing and the chief god of Sidon

tiles.label: Ninisina
tiles.quote: Ninisina was the Mesopotamian goddess of healing and the patron deity of the city of Isin, 'Lady of Isin'

tiles.label: Angitia
tiles.quote: Angitia was an Italic goddess of healing and of snakes, worshipped especially by the Marsi around the Fucine Lake in central Italy

tiles.label: Imhotep
tiles.quote: Centuries later he was revered as a sage and healer and deified, and the Greeks identified him with Asclepius.

tiles.label: Isis
tiles.quote: Isis was a major goddess of ancient Egypt, the wife of Osiris and mother of Horus, revered as a protector of kingship, a healer and a model of devoted motherhood

note: Eshmun is also in Gods of Phoenicia and Carthage; Isis's entry calls her a healer among other roles

tiles.label: Zeus
tiles.quote: Zeus was the chief god of the ancient Greek pantheon, ruler of the sky and of the Olympian gods, and guardian of oaths, hospitality and kingship

tiles.label: Indra
tiles.quote: Indra is the king of the gods in the Rigveda, the god of thunder and rain who wields the thunderbolt and slays the serpent Vritra to release the waters

tiles.label: Enlil
tiles.quote: Enlil was the chief god of the Sumerian pantheon, lord of the wind and air, whose temple, the Ekur, stood at Nippur

tiles.label: Ashur
tiles.quote: Ashur was the chief god of the Assyrians, originally the deity of the city of Ashur on the Tigris, with which he shared his name

tiles.label: Almaqah
tiles.quote: Almaqah was the chief god of the ancient South Arabian kingdom of Saba, worshipped as the national deity of the Sabaeans

tiles.label: Teshub
tiles.quote: Worshipped across northern Mesopotamia, Syria and Anatolia, he was identified with the Hittite storm god and became the chief god of the Hittite state religion

tiles.label: Parmenides
tiles.quote: late 6th–5th century BCE

tiles.label: Ahura Mazda
tiles.quote: Ahura Mazda, also known as Ormazd and Horomazes, is the principal God and sky deity of Zoroastrianism and the spirit most often invoked in the Yasna; the words Ahura and Mazda mean lord and wisdom

tiles.label: Zoroaster
tiles.quote: Zoroaster was the prophet of ancient Iran whose hymns, the Gathas, stand at the origin of Zoroastrianism, among the world's oldest revealed religions

tiles.label: Magi
tiles.quote: The magi (singular magus) were priests in Zoroastrianism and earlier Iranian religions

tiles.label: Fire temple
tiles.quote: A fire temple is a place of worship in Zoroastrianism, where a sacred fire is kept burning

tiles.label: Adur Gushnasp
tiles.quote: Adur Gushnasp was one of the three great sacred fires of Zoroastrian Iran, associated with the warrior class and the kings

tiles.label: Anahita
tiles.quote: Anahita is an ancient Iranian goddess of waters, fertility and healing, invoked in the Avesta as Aredvi Sura Anahita

name: Rulers of Kush

tiles.label: Piye
tiles.quote: Piye, also known as Piankhi, was a king of Kush in the eighth century BCE and successor of Kashta

tiles.label: Taharqa
tiles.quote: Taharqa was a king of Kush and pharaoh of Egypt of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty in the seventh century BCE, one of the most powerful Kushite rulers

tiles.label: Shabaka
tiles.quote: Shabaka was a king of Kush and pharaoh of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, who ruled in the late 8th century BCE

tiles.label: Kashta
tiles.quote: Kashta was a king of Kush in the eighth century BCE who extended Kushite authority into Upper Egypt

tiles.label: Tantamani
tiles.quote: Tantamani was the last king of the Kushite 25th Dynasty to rule Egypt

tiles.label: Amanirenas
tiles.quote: Amanirenas was a ruling queen, or kandake, of the Kingdom of Kush at Meroë

note: Amanirenas is a ruling queen (also in Queens who went to war)

tiles.label: Arsaces I
tiles.quote: Arsaces I was the founder of the Arsacid dynasty and of the Parthian state, who seized the region of Parthia from Seleucid control around 247 BCE

tiles.label: Mithridates I
tiles.quote: Mithridates I was king of Parthia from about 171 to 132 BCE and is regarded as the founder of the Parthian Empire as a major power

tiles.label: Mithridates II
tiles.quote: Mithridates II was king of the Parthian Empire from about 124 to 91 BCE

tiles.label: Phraates II
tiles.quote: Phraates II was a king of the Parthian Empire in the second half of the second century BCE, son of Mithridates I

tiles.label: Vologases VI
tiles.quote: Vologases VI was a king of the Parthian Empire who reigned from about 208 to 228 CE

tiles.label: Artabanus IV
tiles.quote: Artabanus IV was the last king of the Parthian Empire

tiles.label: Croesus
tiles.quote: Croesus was the last king of Lydia in western Anatolia, ruling in the sixth century BCE and proverbial for his wealth

tiles.label: Gyges
tiles.quote: Gyges was king of Lydia from around 680 BCE and founder of the Mermnad dynasty

tiles.label: Alyattes
tiles.quote: Alyattes was king of Lydia from around 610 to 560 BCE, of the Mermnad dynasty, and father of Croesus

tiles.label: Candaules
tiles.quote: Candaules was the last king of the Heraclid dynasty of Lydia, killed around 680 BCE by Gyges, who founded the Mermnad dynasty

tiles.label: Pactolus
tiles.quote: The Pactolus is a small river in western Turkey that flows from Mount Tmolus past the ruins of Sardis into the Gediz, the ancient Hermus

tiles.label: Sardis
tiles.quote: Sardis was the capital of the kingdom of Lydia in western Anatolia

tiles.label: Helots
tiles.quote: The helots were a subjugated group who formed most of the population of Laconia and Messenia, the territories ruled by Sparta; tied to the land, they farmed it to support the Spartan citizens

tiles.label: Perioeci
tiles.quote: The perioeci, "those dwelling around", were the second-tier citizens of Sparta until about 200 BCE, free people living in several dozen dependent cities, mostly in Laconia and Messenia

tiles.label: Agoge
tiles.quote: The agoge was the training programme required for Spartiate, or citizen, status in ancient Sparta

tiles.label: Ephor
tiles.quote: Ephor was the title of senior magistrates, best known from Sparta, who supervised the conduct of kings and officials

tiles.label: Gerousia
tiles.quote: The Gerousia, also called the Spartan Senate, was the council of elders of the ancient Greek city-state of Sparta

tiles.label: Spartiates
tiles.quote: The Spartiates were the full citizens of ancient Sparta, also called homoioi (peers)

tiles.label: Anthony the Great
tiles.quote: Disciples gathered around him, and he is regarded as a founder of Christian monasticism

tiles.label: Pachomius
tiles.quote: Pachomius was an Egyptian Christian monk who founded the first communal monasteries, beginning at Tabennisi in Upper Egypt in the 320s

tiles.label: Columba
tiles.quote: Columba, or Colm Cille, was an Irish monk of the Cenél Conaill, a branch of the northern Uí Néill, who founded the monastery of Iona off western Scotland around 563

tiles.label: Columbanus
tiles.quote: Columbanus was an Irish monk from Bangor who travelled to Gaul around 590 and founded monasteries at Annegray, Luxeuil and Fontaine in the Frankish kingdom of Burgundy

tiles.label: Martin of Tours
tiles.quote: Born in Pannonia, he is remembered for sharing his cloak with a beggar at Amiens, and he founded the monasteries of Ligugé and Marmoutier

tiles.label: Saint Gall
tiles.quote: Saint Gall was a missionary monk, traditionally said to be an Irish companion of Saint Columbanus, who around 612 settled as a hermit in the Steinach valley south of Lake Constance

name: Cut into rock

tiles.label: Naqsh-e Rostam
tiles.quote: It contains the rock-cut tombs of Achaemenid kings and later Sasanian rock reliefs

tiles.label: Bamiyan Buddhas
tiles.quote: The Buddhas of Bamiyan were two monumental standing Buddha statues, 55 and 38 metres tall, carved into a cliff in the Bamiyan valley of central Afghanistan in the 6th century

tiles.label: Abu Simbel
tiles.quote: Abu Simbel is a site on the Nile in Lower Nubia, southern Egypt, with two rock-cut temples built by Ramesses II in the 13th century BCE; the larger is fronted by four colossal seated statues of the king

tiles.label: Kizil
tiles.quote: The Kizil Caves are a complex of more than 230 Buddhist rock-cut caves near Kucha in Xinjiang, China, carved into cliffs above the Muzat River between about the 3rd and 8th centuries

tiles.label: Al-Khazneh
tiles.quote: Al-Khazneh, 'the Treasury', is a monumental facade carved into the sandstone cliff at the end of the Siq gorge in Petra, Jordan

tiles.label: Beni Hasan
tiles.quote: Its rock-cut tombs of the Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasties belonged to the nomarchs of the Oryx nome, and their paintings show daily life, wrestling, warfare and a caravan of Asiatic traders in the tomb of Khnumhotep II

note: Kizil and the Bamiyan Buddhas run past 600 CE; Ellora (c. 600-1000) and Ajanta would also fit

tiles.label: Marib
tiles.quote: The Marib Dam was an ancient dam across the Wadi Adhanah near Marib in Yemen, built to capture seasonal floods and irrigate two large oases

tiles.label: Eupalinos
tiles.quote: The Tunnel of Eupalinos is an aqueduct tunnel 1,036 metres long cut through Mount Kastro on Samos in the sixth century BCE, under the tyrant Polycrates

tiles.label: Band-e Kaisar
tiles.quote: The Band-e Kaisar was a combined bridge and dam on the Karun River at Shushtar in south-western Iran, built under the Sasanian Empire in the third century

tiles.label: Siloam
tiles.quote: The Siloam tunnel, also called Hezekiah's tunnel, is an ancient water channel about 533 metres long cut through the rock beneath the City of David in Jerusalem

tiles.label: Foggara
tiles.quote: A foggara is an underground irrigation tunnel that taps groundwater and carries it by gravity to the surface, similar to the Persian qanat

tiles.label: Proserpina
tiles.quote: The Proserpina Dam is a Roman gravity dam near Mérida in Spain, built probably in the 1st or 2nd century CE to supply Emerita Augusta, capital of Lusitania

name: First known in Mesopotamia

tiles.label: Cuneiform
tiles.quote: Cuneiform is a writing system of wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay tablets, invented in Mesopotamia in the late fourth millennium BCE

tiles.label: Sexagesimal
tiles.quote: Sexagesimal, or base 60, is a numeral system with sixty as its base, which originated with the Sumerians in the 3rd millennium BCE and passed to the Babylonians

tiles.label: Abacus
tiles.quote: first known in Sumer, where it appeared between 2700 and 2300 BCE

tiles.label: Soap
tiles.quote: Soap is a salt of a fatty acid, often made by mixing fats or oils with an alkali, used for washing and cleaning; the earliest recorded evidence of soap-like materials comes from Mesopotamia, c

tiles.label: Distillation
tiles.quote: Akkadian tablets of c. 1200 BCE describing perfumery show that a primitive form was known to the Babylonians of Mesopotamia

tiles.label: Seed drill
tiles.quote: A seed drill is a device that sows seeds by placing them in the soil at a set depth; the Babylonians used primitive seed drills around 1400 BCE

note: Keep apart from Ancient inventions (wheel, sail also have Mesopotamian evidence)

tiles.label: Apollo of Veii
tiles.quote: It is one of the masterpieces of Etruscan art and is displayed in the National Etruscan Museum at the Villa Giulia in Rome.

tiles.label: Chimera of Arezzo
tiles.quote: The Chimera of Arezzo is an Etruscan bronze statue of the mythical fire-breathing lion with a goat's head rising from its back and a serpent for a tail, made around 400 BCE

tiles.label: Sarcophagus of the Spouses
tiles.quote: The Sarcophagus of the Spouses is an Etruscan terracotta funerary urn from Caere, made around 520 BCE, showing a married couple reclining together at a banquet

tiles.label: Liber Linteus
tiles.quote: The Liber Linteus, or Linen Book of Zagreb, is the longest surviving Etruscan text and the only surviving linen book, written about 250 BCE, probably in south-eastern Tuscany near Lake Trasimeno

tiles.label: Liver of Piacenza
tiles.quote: The Liver of Piacenza is a life-sized bronze model of a sheep's liver inscribed in Etruscan, dated to the late 2nd century BCE and found in 1877 near Gossolengo in the province of Piacenza, Italy

tiles.label: Pyrgi Tablets
tiles.quote: The Pyrgi Tablets are three gold plates of about 500 BCE, two inscribed in Etruscan and one in Phoenician, found in 1964 at ancient Pyrgi, on the Tyrrhenian coast of Lazio

tiles.label: Rosetta Stone
tiles.quote: The Rosetta Stone is a granodiorite slab inscribed with a decree issued at Memphis in 196 BCE in the name of the Ptolemaic king Ptolemy V, written in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic script and ancient Greek

tiles.label: Behistun
tiles.quote: The Behistun Inscription is a monumental rock relief and text carved on a cliff in western Iran on the orders of the Achaemenid king Darius I, recording his accession and victories

tiles.label: Mesha Stele
tiles.quote: The Mesha Stele, or Moabite Stone, is a basalt slab inscribed around 840 BCE for King Mesha of Moab, found at Dhiban in Jordan in 1868 and now in the Louvre

tiles.label: Tel Dan Stele
tiles.quote: The Tel Dan stele is a fragmentary Aramaic inscription of the 9th century BCE found in 1993–1994 at Tel Dan in northern Israel

tiles.label: Edicts of Ashoka
tiles.quote: The Edicts of Ashoka are a series of inscriptions on rocks and pillars issued by the Maurya emperor Ashoka in the third century BCE

tiles.label: Gwanggaeto Stele
tiles.quote: Its inscription of some 1,800 Chinese characters records Goguryeo's founding legend, Gwanggaeto's campaigns, including an expedition of 400 to help Silla against the Wa, and lists of tomb-guard households.

tiles.label: Strabo
tiles.quote: Strabo was a Greek geographer and historian from Amaseia in Pontus, active under Augustus and Tiberius

tiles.label: Ptolemy
tiles.quote: Claudius Ptolemy was a Greek mathematician, astronomer and geographer who worked in Alexandria in the second century CE

tiles.label: Eratosthenes
tiles.quote: He made a remarkably close estimate of the Earth's circumference from the angle of the sun at Syene and Alexandria, drew a map of the known world with lines of latitude and longitude, and devised a method for finding prime numbers

tiles.label: Pausanias
tiles.quote: Pausanias was a Greek traveller and geographer of the 2nd century CE, probably from Asia Minor

tiles.label: Marinus of Tyre
tiles.quote: Marinus of Tyre was a Greek geographer and mapmaker of the Roman period, active around 100 CE

tiles.label: Hecataeus
tiles.quote: Hecataeus of Miletus was an early Greek historian and geographer

name: War elephants

tiles.label: Hydaspes
tiles.quote: Alexander crossed the swollen river upstream of Porus' army under cover of a storm and defeated it despite its war elephants

tiles.label: Ipsus
tiles.quote: Seleucus's war elephants played an important role, and Antigonus was killed

tiles.label: Porus
tiles.quote: In 326 BCE he fought Alexander the Great at the Battle of the Hydaspes with a large army including war elephants, and was defeated

tiles.label: Chandragupta
tiles.quote: He extended his rule across northern India and fought Seleucus I, gaining territories in the northwest in exchange for 500 war elephants

tiles.label: Seleucid–Mauryan war
tiles.quote: Seleucus ceded territories in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent and received a large number of war elephants in return

tiles.label: Crossing of the Alps
tiles.quote: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps was the march of a Carthaginian army, including war elephants, from Iberia over the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE

note: Hannibal (Carthaginians) and Chandragupta would make good decoys elsewhere

name: All in 480 BCE

tiles.label: Thermopylae
tiles.quote: The Battle of Thermopylae was fought in 480 BCE at a narrow coastal pass in central Greece, where a small Greek force led by King Leonidas of Sparta held off the army of Xerxes I for several days

tiles.label: Salamis
tiles.quote: The Battle of Salamis was a naval battle fought in 480 BCE in the straits between the island of Salamis and the coast of Attica, during the second Persian invasion of Greece

tiles.label: Artemisium
tiles.quote: The Battle of Artemisium was a series of naval engagements fought over three days in August 480 BCE off the northern tip of Euboea, at the same time as the land battle at Thermopylae

tiles.label: Gelon
tiles.quote: With Theron of Acragas he crushed the Carthaginians at the Battle of Himera in 480 BCE.

tiles.label: Leonidas
tiles.quote: Leonidas I was a king of Sparta of the Agiad line who commanded the Greek force defending the pass of Thermopylae against the Persian invasion of Xerxes in 480 BCE

tiles.label: Acropolis
tiles.quote: After the Persians sacked it in 480 BCE it was rebuilt under Pericles with the Parthenon, the Propylaea, the Erechtheion and the Temple of Athena Nike

note: Thermopylae, Salamis and Artemisium are also battles of the Greco-Persian Wars (published group); Gelon's Himera is the decoy-free tile

tiles.label: Babylon
tiles.quote: It was conquered by Cyrus the Great in 539 BCE and remained an important centre under the Achaemenid and Seleucid empires.

tiles.label: Nabonidus
tiles.quote: His unpopularity contributed to the empire's fall to Cyrus the Great of Persia in 539 BCE.

tiles.label: Belshazzar
tiles.quote: He probably died when the Persians took the city in 539 BCE.

tiles.label: Babylonian captivity
tiles.quote: The exile ended after the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, when Cyrus allowed the exiles to return

tiles.label: Chaldean Empire
tiles.quote: It was conquered by Cyrus the Great of the Achaemenid Empire in 539 BCE.

tiles.label: Opis
tiles.quote: The Battle of Opis was fought in 539 BCE near the Tigris in Mesopotamia, where the Persian forces of Cyrus the Great defeated the Babylonian army

tiles.label: Nineveh
tiles.quote: Its capture and destruction in 612 BCE by a coalition of the Median Empire and Babylonians led by Nabopolassar marked the fall of Assyria.

tiles.label: Median Empire
tiles.quote: In alliance with Babylon, the Medes destroyed the Assyrian Empire, capturing Nineveh in 612 BCE

tiles.label: Assyrian Empire
tiles.quote: The Neo-Assyrian Empire was the final and greatest phase of Assyrian power, beginning with a revival after 911 BCE and ending with the fall of Nineveh in 612 BCE

tiles.label: Cyaxares
tiles.quote: Allied with Nabopolassar of Babylon, he sacked Assur in 614 BCE and helped destroy Nineveh in 612 BCE

tiles.label: Ashur-uballit II
tiles.quote: After the fall of Nineveh to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BCE, he tried to continue resistance from Harran with Egyptian support

tiles.label: Medo-Babylonian alliance
tiles.quote: Together they captured Nineveh in 612 BCE and destroyed the Assyrian Empire

tiles.label: Chaeronea
tiles.quote: The Battle of Chaeronea was fought in Boeotia in August 338 BCE between Philip II of Macedon and an alliance led by Athens and Thebes

tiles.label: Artaxerxes III
tiles.quote: Artaxerxes III was an Achaemenid king who reigned from 358 BCE until he was assassinated in 338 BCE

tiles.label: Latin War
tiles.quote: The Latin War of 340–338 BCE was fought between Rome and its former allies of the Latin League, joined by the Campanians and Volsci

tiles.label: Archidamus III
tiles.quote: Archidamus III was king of Sparta from about 360 to 338 BCE, son of Agesilaus II

tiles.label: Duke Xiao of Qin
tiles.quote: Duke Xiao of Qin ruled the State of Qin from 361 to 338 BCE

tiles.label: Antium
tiles.quote: A Volscian port whose ships raided the coast, it resisted Rome until 338 BCE, when its fleet was taken and the bronze prows (rostra) of its ships were set up on the speakers' platform in the Roman Forum

tiles.label: Peloponnesian War
tiles.quote: The Peloponnesian War was fought from 431 to 404 BCE between Athens and its empire and the Peloponnesian League led by Sparta

tiles.label: Delian League
tiles.quote: It was dissolved after Athens' defeat in the Peloponnesian War in 404 BCE.

tiles.label: Thirty Tyrants
tiles.quote: The Thirty Tyrants were the oligarchy of thirty men installed in Athens with Spartan backing after its defeat in the Peloponnesian War in 404 BCE

tiles.label: Amyrtaeus
tiles.quote: On the death of Darius II in 404 BCE he led a revolt that ended the first period of Persian rule in Egypt, and by about 400 BCE he was recognised throughout the country

tiles.label: Decelean War
tiles.quote: The Decelean War, also called the Ionian War, was the final phase of the Peloponnesian War, from 413 to 404 BCE

tiles.label: Lysias
tiles.quote: In 404 BCE the Thirty Tyrants made Polemarchus drink hemlock, and Lysias escaped to Megara with the help of a bribe

name: All in 168 BCE

tiles.label: Perseus of Macedon
tiles.quote: Perseus was the last king of the Antigonid dynasty of Macedonia, son of Philip V, reigning from 179 to 168 BCE

tiles.label: Antigonid dynasty
tiles.quote: It ruled Macedonia from the third century BCE until the Roman conquest in 168 BCE

tiles.label: Gentius
tiles.quote: Allied with Perseus of Macedon in the Third Macedonian War, he was defeated by the Roman praetor Lucius Anicius Gallus in 168 BCE, captured at Scodra and led in triumph at Rome

tiles.label: Ptolemy VI
tiles.quote: He survived the invasion of Antiochus IV, which Rome halted in 168 BCE, and through Roman arbitration his brother received Cyrenaica in 163 BCE

tiles.label: Shkodër
tiles.quote: As Scodra it was the capital of the Illyrian king Gentius, captured by Rome in 168 BCE

tiles.label: Pydna
tiles.quote: The Battle of Pydna was fought on 22 June 168 BCE near Pydna in Macedonia, where a Roman army under Lucius Aemilius Paullus defeated King Perseus of Macedon

note: Pydna is a battle Macedonicus (Named after the lands) won

tiles.label: Cambyses II
tiles.quote: He conquered Egypt after defeating Pharaoh Psamtik III at the Battle of Pelusium in 525 BCE

tiles.label: Pelusium
tiles.quote: The Battle of Pelusium was fought in 525 BCE at the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, where the Persian king Cambyses II defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III

tiles.label: Psamtik III
tiles.quote: He was defeated by the Persian king Cambyses II at the Battle of Pelusium in 525 BCE

tiles.label: 27th Dynasty
tiles.quote: The Twenty-seventh Dynasty of Egypt is the name given to the first period of Persian rule over Egypt, beginning with Cambyses II's conquest in 525 BCE

tiles.label: Siphnian Treasury
tiles.quote: The Siphnian Treasury is a small Ionic building at the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi, built about 525 BCE by the people of Siphnos from the wealth of their gold and silver mines

tiles.label: Udjahorresnet
tiles.quote: His inscribed statue, now in the Vatican Museums, records that he helped Cambyses II compose his pharaonic titles after the conquest of 525 BCE and that Darius I sent him to restore the medical school at Sais.

tiles.label: Shapur I
tiles.quote: He defeated several Roman emperors, capturing Antioch and taking Emperor Valerian prisoner at Edessa in 260 CE

tiles.label: Valerian
tiles.quote: In 260 CE he was captured by the Sasanian king Shapur I after the Battle of Edessa, becoming the first Roman emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy

tiles.label: Gallienus
tiles.quote: Gallienus was Roman emperor from 253 to 268, first with his father Valerian and alone after Valerian's capture by the Persians in 260

tiles.label: Gallic Empire
tiles.quote: The Gallic Empire was a breakaway state in the western provinces of the Roman Empire, including Gaul, Britain and for a time Spain, from 260 to 274 CE

tiles.label: Postumus
tiles.quote: A commander on the Rhine, he was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 260, after Valerian's capture by the Persians, and killed Gallienus' son Saloninus at Cologne

tiles.label: Odaenathus
tiles.quote: After the Persian king Shapur I captured the emperor Valerian in 260, he attacked the retreating Persian army, suppressed the usurpers Macrianus and Quietus, and raided Sasanian territory as far as Ctesiphon

name: All in 395

tiles.label: Theodosius I
tiles.quote: Theodosius I was a Roman emperor who died in 395 CE, the last to rule both the eastern and western halves of the empire

tiles.label: Augustine
tiles.quote: After teaching rhetoric in Carthage, Rome and Milan, he converted to Christianity in 386 and became bishop of Hippo Regius in 395, where he wrote against the Donatists and Pelagians

tiles.label: Western Roman Empire
tiles.quote: The Western Roman Empire was the western half of the Roman Empire, governed separately after the permanent division of 395 CE

tiles.label: Arcadius
tiles.quote: Arcadius was Roman emperor in the East from 395 to 408, the elder son of Theodosius I

tiles.label: Canhe Slope
tiles.quote: The Battle of Canhe Slope was fought in 395 in northern China between the Later Yan army of Murong Bao and the forces of Tuoba Gui of Northern Wei

tiles.label: Stilicho
tiles.quote: effectively governed the western empire for the young emperor Honorius from 395

note: Mixes Rome, Augustine and a Chinese battle

tiles.label: Göktürks
tiles.quote: The Göktürk Khaganate was a Turkic empire founded by the Ashina clan in 552, which came to dominate the Eurasian steppe from Manchuria to the Black Sea

tiles.label: Hou Jing
tiles.quote: He proclaimed himself emperor of Han in 551 but was defeated by Liang forces under Wang Sengbian and Chen Baxian and killed in 552

tiles.label: Emperor Yuan of Liang
tiles.quote: Emperor Yuan of Liang, Xiao Yi, a son of Emperor Wu of Liang and a noted scholar, crushed the rebel Hou Jing and took the throne at Jiangling in 552

tiles.label: Taginae
tiles.quote: The Battle of Taginae, also called Busta Gallorum, was fought in the Apennines of central Italy in the summer of 552

tiles.label: Totila
tiles.quote: Totila, also called Baduila, was king of the Ostrogoths from 541 to 552

tiles.label: Teia
tiles.quote: Teia was the last king of the Ostrogoths in Italy, elected after Totila's death at Taginae in 552

name: End in -cles

tiles.label: Heracles
tiles.quote: Heracles, called Hercules by the Romans, was the greatest hero of Greek myth, a son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene

tiles.label: Themistocles
tiles.quote: Themistocles was an Athenian statesman and general who persuaded Athens to build a large fleet with the silver of Laurion

tiles.label: Agathocles
tiles.quote: Agathocles of Syracuse seized power as tyrant of Syracuse in 317 BCE and later took the title of king

tiles.label: Pericles
tiles.quote: Pericles was an Athenian statesman and general who dominated the democracy from the 450s until his death in 429 BCE

tiles.label: Sophocles
tiles.quote: Sophocles was an Athenian tragic playwright who lived from about 497 to 406 BCE

tiles.label: Empedocles
tiles.quote: Empedocles was a Greek philosopher, poet and statesman from Acragas in Sicily

note: Pericles and Sophocles are also Athenians; Empedocles a philosopher before Socrates

name: End in -ates

tiles.label: Hippocrates
tiles.quote: Hippocrates was a Greek physician from the island of Kos, born around 460 BCE, who is traditionally called the father of medicine

tiles.label: Mithridates VI
tiles.quote: Mithridates VI Eupator was king of Pontus from about 120 BCE and Rome's most persistent enemy in the east

tiles.label: Euphrates
tiles.quote: The Euphrates is one of the two great rivers of Mesopotamia, flowing from Anatolia through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf

tiles.label: Tiridates I
tiles.quote: Tiridates I was king of Armenia in the mid-1st century CE and founder of the Arsacid dynasty of Armenia

tiles.label: Isocrates
tiles.quote: Isocrates was an Athenian orator and teacher of rhetoric

tiles.label: Socrates
tiles.quote: Socrates was an Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing himself but questioned his fellow citizens about justice, virtue and knowledge, a method of inquiry known through the dialogues of his pupil Plato and the writings of Xenophon

note: Euphrates (a river) is the surprise; Socrates is also an Athenian

name: End in -ander

tiles.label: Alexander
tiles.quote: Alexander the Great, Alexander III of Macedon, was king of Macedon from 336 to 323 BCE

tiles.label: Cassander
tiles.quote: Cassander was a Macedonian general and ruler of Macedonia after the death of Alexander the Great, one of the Diadochi who fought over Alexander's empire

tiles.label: Periander
tiles.quote: Periander was tyrant of Corinth from about 627 to 587 BCE, son and successor of Cypselus

tiles.label: Menander I
tiles.quote: Menander I was the best-known Indo-Greek king, ruling much of the Punjab and Gandhara from Sagala in the mid-2nd century BCE

tiles.label: Lysander
tiles.quote: Lysander was a Spartan admiral and statesman who won the Peloponnesian War for Sparta

tiles.label: Anaximander
tiles.quote: Anaximander of Miletus was a Greek philosopher of the 6th century BCE and a pupil of Thales in the Milesian school

note: Lysander also in the Peloponnesian War; Anaximander before Socrates

tiles.label: Heliopolis
tiles.quote: Heliopolis, Egyptian Iunu and biblical On, was one of the oldest cities of ancient Egypt, now within north-eastern Cairo, and the chief cult centre of the sun god Ra and of Atum

tiles.label: Hermopolis
tiles.quote: Hermopolis, ancient Egyptian Khemenu and modern el-Ashmunein, was a city in Middle Egypt and the chief cult centre of Thoth, god of wisdom and writing

tiles.label: Herakleopolis
tiles.quote: Herakleopolis Magna was an ancient Egyptian city south of the Faiyum, near modern Beni Suef, and capital of the 20th nome of Upper Egypt

tiles.label: Nicopolis
tiles.quote: Nicopolis was a city in Epirus, on the peninsula north of modern Preveza in western Greece, founded by Octavian (Augustus) to commemorate his victory over Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE

tiles.label: Seuthopolis
tiles.quote: Seuthopolis was the capital founded around 320 BCE by the Odrysian king Seuthes III in the Kazanlak valley of central Bulgaria

tiles.label: Persepolis
tiles.quote: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, located in Fars in south-western Iran and begun under Darius I

name: Claimed the Roman throne from Britain

tiles.label: Carausius
tiles.quote: Accused of keeping captured plunder, he declared himself emperor in 286 and ruled Britain and part of northern Gaul until he was murdered in 293 by his finance minister Allectus.

tiles.label: Allectus
tiles.quote: Allectus was a Roman usurper who ruled Britain from 293 to 296

tiles.label: Magnus Maximus
tiles.quote: Magnus Maximus was a Roman general of Spanish origin who, as commander in Britain, was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 383

tiles.label: Constantine III
tiles.quote: Constantine III was a common soldier proclaimed emperor by the Roman army in Britain in 407

tiles.label: Clodius Albinus
tiles.quote: Clodius Albinus was governor of Britain who claimed the Roman throne in the civil wars after 193

note: Only five candidates; Constantine I (proclaimed at York, in Constantius I's entry) is a near miss

name: Named after the lands they fought

tiles.label: Germanicus
tiles.quote: From 14 to 16 CE he led campaigns across the Rhine against Arminius and the Germanic peoples, visiting the site of the Teutoburg disaster and recovering two of Varus' lost eagles, but made no lasting conquest

tiles.label: Africanus
tiles.quote: He captured Carthago Nova in 209 BCE, won at Ilipa in 206 BCE, driving the Carthaginians from Iberia, and in 204 BCE invaded Africa with Masinissa as ally

tiles.label: Achaicus
tiles.quote: Lucius Mummius Achaicus was a Roman consul and general who defeated the Achaean League in 146 BCE

tiles.label: Macedonicus
tiles.quote: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus was a Roman general who defeated King Perseus of Macedon at Pydna in 168 BCE, ending the Third Macedonian War and the Antigonid monarchy

tiles.label: Gothicus
tiles.quote: Soon after his accession he defeated an Alemannic army near Lake Garda, and around 269 he won a great victory over the Goths at Naissus, which earned him his surname

note: Five candidates; the labels are the victory names (Metellus Numidicus, Balearicus, Creticus exist but weigh 0)

name: Languages with no known relatives

tiles.label: Sumerian
tiles.quote: It is unrelated to any known language

tiles.label: Elamite
tiles.quote: It has no known relatives

tiles.label: Hattic
tiles.quote: It is unrelated to the Indo-European Hittite language and to the Semitic languages and has no known relatives

tiles.label: Burushaski
tiles.quote: It is a language isolate, with no proven relationship to any other language

tiles.label: Basque
tiles.quote: The Basques are a people of the western Pyrenees, in northern Spain and south-western France, with a distinct language unrelated to other European languages

tiles.label: Hurrian
tiles.quote: The Hurrians were a people of the ancient Near East, speaking a language unrelated to Semitic or Indo-European tongues, who were widespread in northern Mesopotamia, Syria and Anatolia

note: Basque and Hurrian entries are peoples whose language is described as unrelated; Burushaski is modern
